title: Letters to Egypt and the Hidden Fire
sum: 2 Maccabees does not open with its story but with two letters from Judea to the Jews of Egypt. The first (1:1–9) is short: it wishes its readers God's favor, recalls an earlier letter written in 143 BC, "in the trouble and the crisis" that followed Jason's revolt, and urges them to keep "the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev," the feast now called Hanukkah. In Swete's punctuation it ends with its date, the year 188 (Venetus; Swete's text has 88), which is 124 BC.

The second letter (1:10–2:18) claims to come from Judas, the council of elders and the people of Judea, writing to Aristobulus, a Jewish teacher at the court of Ptolemy. It thanks God for the death of Antiochus, who, it says, was stoned and cut up by the priests of the goddess Nanea when he came to plunder her temple. Then it tells a story to explain the feast: the fire of the first temple, hidden in a dry well at the exile, was found by Nehemiah's priests as a thick liquid that burst into flame when the sun shone on it. A long prayer, with a string of titles for God, asks him to gather his scattered people and plant them in his holy place.
readings: Both letters belong to a known kind: letters to Jews abroad about the dates and keeping of feasts. The Greek Esther ends with a note that a letter about Purim was brought to Egypt from Jerusalem, and a papyrus from Elephantine in Egypt, about 419 BC, preserves a letter from one Hananiah on keeping the Passover. Read this way, the chapter is less a history than an invitation to keep a feast together.
Read as a story of continuity

The fire story makes a claim. The temple Judas purified is not a new temple but the old one, with the same fire that came down from heaven in Moses' and Solomon's day. Hanukkah is joined to Booths, to Nehemiah and to Solomon (2:9–12), so that the youngest feast in Israel's calendar has the oldest roots.

views.C: Catholic readers receive the letters as part of the inspired book, and Catholic interpreters weigh what kind of writing each passage is (Catechism 110): a letter that reports how a pagan king was rumored to have died need not settle the facts against chapter 9. The prayer of 1:24–29, with its titles of God and its plea for the scattered people, is valued as a model of Jewish prayer near the time of Christ.
views.O: Orthodox Bibles, which follow the Septuagint, include the letters with the rest of 2 Maccabees. Orthodox readers have taken the fire story, like the ark story in chapter 2, as a witness that the worship of the second temple stood in one line with that of the tabernacle, and that God keeps his holy things for his people.
views.P: Protestant churches place the book among the Apocrypha. The Westminster Confession (1.3) holds such books to be no part of the canon, to be used only as other human writings. Protestant readers point to this chapter for reasons: its account of Antiochus's death does not agree with chapter 9, and its Nehemiah builds the temple, against Ezra 3 and 6.
views.H: Most historians, following Elias Bickerman (1933), take the first letter, dated 124 BC, as a genuine letter, perhaps with an earlier one inside it. Most doubt that the second letter is from Judas, since its account of Antiochus's death conflicts with the book and with Polybius, and it shares the book's legendary style. Ben Zion Wacholder (1978) defended it as a genuine letter of Judas's lifetime.
views.J: The rabbis did not preserve 2 Maccabees, and their Hanukkah is a feast of lights. The Talmud explains it with the story of a single jar of pure oil that burned for eight days (Bavli Shabbat 21b). Josephus already calls the feast "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325). The letter's link between the feast and a sacred fire is close to that later theme, but its story of Nehemiah's fire is not told by the rabbis.

deep.h: Two letters: their dates and authenticity
deep.b:
Where does each letter begin and end? Swete's punctuation, which most editors since Bickerman follow, gives a first letter of 1:1–10a, closing with the date, the year 188 (124 BC; Swete's text has 88, Venetus 188), and a second of 1:10b–2:18. Rahlfs also ends 1:9 with the date. The first letter mentions an earlier one of 169 SE (143/142 BC). Some scholars think 1:7–8 quotes that earlier letter; others that it only recalls it. Venetus, the Vulgate and the KJV join the date to the second letter instead (see the variants).

The first letter is plain, its Greek reads like a translation of Hebrew or Aramaic, and its date fits the known practice of festal letters. Most accept it as genuine. The second is another matter. It claims to come from Judas, who died in 160 BC, and it must be dated after Antiochus's death in late 164 BC, yet before the feast it announces. Its account of the death conflicts with chapter 9, and it is full of legend. Most scholars think it was composed later in Judas's name, perhaps in the first century BC. Wacholder argued that it is a genuine letter of Judas's lifetime, written before the facts of the king's death were known in Jerusalem.

Why attach them to the book? Both press the Jews of Egypt to keep Hanukkah, and the book that follows tells how the feast began. Whoever joined them made the history serve the feast.

deep.h: The three deaths of Antiochus IV
deep.b:
The Jewish sources give three accounts. In this letter, Antiochus is trapped and stoned in the temple of Nanea (1:13–16). In 1 Maccabees 6:1–16 he fails to take a rich temple in Elymais, hears that his armies in Judea have been beaten, falls sick with grief and dies, confessing the evils he did in Jerusalem. In 2 Maccabees 9 he is struck by God with pains in his bowels, falls from his chariot, rots alive, and makes vows and a letter before he dies.

Polybius, a Greek contemporary, says Antiochus tried to rob a temple of Artemis in Elymais, was driven off by the local people, and died at Tabae in Persia, "out of his mind," as some said, because of signs from the gods (Histories 31.9). Josephus prefers 1 Maccabees and says it is more likely that he died for the temple at Jerusalem than for the one he only planned to rob (Antiquities 12.354–359). Antiochus III, his father, was killed in 187 BC while plundering a temple of Bel in Elymais, which may have colored the letter's story.

Historians accept the outline that 1 Maccabees and Polybius share: a failed temple raid in the east, then illness and death late in 164 BC. A Babylonian king list records that news of his death was heard in Babylon in year 148 SE, probably in Kislev (the month is restored on the tablet). That is close to the time of the temple's purification in Jerusalem, and it explains why the second letter can put the two events together.

The letter makes Nehemiah the builder of the temple and the altar (1:18), a role that Ezra gives to Zerubbabel and Jeshua about 520–515 BC (Ezra 3:2; Ezra 6:15). Nehemiah came in 445 BC and rebuilt the walls. The letter also has priests hide fire "when our ancestors were being led away to Persia," where Babylon is meant. Its interest is not in dates but in continuity: the fire that God sent at the first sacrifice (Leviticus 9:24) and at Solomon's prayer (2 Chronicles 7:1) was never lost.

The story may have grown around naphtha, the crude oil found in seeps in Persia and Mesopotamia, which catches fire easily. The letter even gives the place's name as Nephthar and explains it as "purification" (1:36). Its point is that the God of Israel was honored even by a Persian king, who fenced the place in and made it sacred.

echoes: Exodus 2:24; Leviticus 6:13; Leviticus 9:24; Deuteronomy 30:3–5; Deuteronomy 32:9; Exodus 15:17; 1 Kings 8:60; 1 Kings 18:38; 2 Chronicles 7:1; Ezra 3:2; Ezra 6:15; Nehemiah 1:9; Nehemiah 2:1–8; Nehemiah 9:6; Psalm 147:2; 1 Chronicles 28:9; John 10:22; John 11:52

settings.what: The first letter to the Jews of Egypt
settings.by: "your brothers, the Jews in Jerusalem and in the land of Judea"
settings.when: 124 BC, by the date at its close (1:10a); it recalls a letter of 143/142 BC
settings.why: To ask the Jews of Egypt to keep the new feast of the temple's purification, "the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev," with the Jews of Judea, and to remind them of the covenant they share.
settings.readers: Its first readers were the Jews of Egypt, a large community with its own temple at Leontopolis since the 160s BC, founded by a son of Onias the high priest, as Josephus reports (Antiquities 13.62–73). A letter from Jerusalem urging a Jerusalem feast would remind them where the true temple stood. The Greek Esther closes with a similar note: a letter about Purim was brought to Egypt from Jerusalem in the reign of a Ptolemy and Cleopatra.
views: Most scholars, following Bickerman, accept it as a real letter of 124 BC, translated from Hebrew or Aramaic.
Some think the editor of the book chose and trimmed it, together with the second letter, to introduce the history.

settings.what: The second letter, in the name of Judas (from the second sentence of 1:10)
settings.by: "those in Judea, with the council of elders and Judas"
settings.to: Aristobulus, "the teacher of King Ptolemy," and the Jews in Egypt
settings.when: It sets itself just after Antiochus's death, late 164 BC, before the first Hanukkah
settings.why: To announce the feast of purification and give it a history: the death of the temple's enemy, Nehemiah's fire, Jeremiah's hiding of the tent and ark, and Solomon's eight days. It also offers to send books to Egypt.
settings.readers: If it was composed later, as most think, its readers were Jews in Egypt in the late second or first century BC, the generation for whom Ben Sira's grandson translated his grandfather's book there after 132 BC (Sirach prologue). Clement of Alexandria, about AD 200, still read it with the book and knew Aristobulus from it (Stromata 5.14.97.7).
views: Most scholars think it was written in Judas's name, perhaps in the first century BC, because it conflicts with chapter 9 and is full of legend.
Wacholder argued that it is a real letter of Judas's lifetime, written before full reports of the king's death had reached Jerusalem.

settings.what: The priests' prayer at Nehemiah's sacrifice
settings.when: as the letter tells it, at the first sacrifice in Nehemiah's day
settings.why: To praise God with the titles Greek kings claimed for themselves, and to ask him to accept the sacrifice, keep his people, gather those scattered among the nations, and plant them in his holy place.
settings.readers: The prayer reached its first readers inside a letter addressed to the Jews of Egypt, for whom the plea to "bring our dispersed people together" described their own situation. The letter was still read in Egypt with the book about AD 200, when Clement of Alexandria refers to it (Stromata 5.14.97.7).

title: The Hidden Ark and the Writer's Preface
sum: The second letter goes on with older records. The prophet Jeremiah, it says, told the exiles to take the fire and not to forget the law among the idols of Babylon. On God's word he took the tent, the ark and the altar of incense to the mountain from which Moses saw the land, hid them in a cave and sealed it. When his companions tried to mark the way, he rebuked them: the place will stay unknown "until God gathers his people in," and then the glory and the cloud will be seen again. The letter also links Moses' and Solomon's sacrifices with fire from heaven and Solomon's eight days of dedication, and tells how Nehemiah, and later Judas, gathered the sacred books. It ends with the hope that God will soon gather his people to the holy place.

At 2:19 a new voice begins. The writer explains that he is summarizing the five books of Jason of Cyrene about Judas, the purification of the temple, the wars with Antiochus and his son, and the "appearances from heaven" that helped the Jews. He speaks of his "sweat and sleepless nights," compares himself to a host preparing a banquet and to the decorator of a house, and leaves exact research to the historian.
readings: The ark story fills a silence. The 66 books never say what happened to the ark. Here it is safe, waiting with the people for the end. Like the fire story, the tale ties the second temple to the first and points to a future gathering.

The preface lets the reader see how the book was made: who wrote the first history, what was cut, what the abridger aimed at. Few books of the period say so much about their own method, and this preface is the reason later readers have asked what inspiration means for a book written this way.

views.C: Catholic readers hold the book inspired even though its writer speaks of his labor (2:26–27), since the Church teaches that God used human authors "as true authors" (Dei Verbum 11). Revelation 11:19, where the ark appears in heaven, is read in the liturgy with Revelation 12 on the feast of the Assumption, and the Catechism calls Mary "the ark of the covenant" (2676).
views.O: Orthodox tradition keeps the story of Jeremiah and the ark: the synaxarion (the lives of the saints read in services) for 1 May, the prophet's day, says he hid the ark in a rock and that it will be the first raised at the resurrection, and be set on Mount Sinai. Orthodox hymns call the Mother of God the ark of the covenant.
views.P: Protestant readers point to the preface as evidence that the book is not inspired: a prophet does not apologize for his style or call his work an abridgment. They also note that Jeremiah 3:16 says the ark will not be remembered or made again, which sits uneasily with a hidden ark waiting to be found.
views.H: Historians read the ark story as one of several legends of the period about the temple's lost vessels (compare 2 Baruch 6; the Lives of the Prophets). The library of 2:13–15 is valued as early evidence that Jews spoke of sacred books in groups, though it does not say which books counted. The preface is read as the work of the epitomist, writing in good Hellenistic style.
views.J: The rabbis discussed the ark's fate. Some said Josiah hid it, on the basis of 2 Chronicles 35:3 (Bavli Yoma 52b); others that it was taken to Babylon; the Mishnah tells of a priest who saw an odd stone in the floor of the woodshed chamber and died before he could tell where the ark lay (Mishnah Shekalim 6:1–2). Jeremiah's role is not in these stories.

deep.b:
The last mention of the ark in the narrative books is Josiah's command to put it in the house Solomon built (2 Chronicles 35:3). The list of things Babylon took in 586 BC does not include it (2 Kings 25:13–17). Jeremiah 3:16 looks forward to a day when no one will miss it. The Second Temple had no ark: Josephus says the inner sanctuary held "nothing at all" (Jewish War 5.219).

Several stories filled the gap. 2 Maccabees gives it to Jeremiah, who hides it on Mount Nebo. 2 Baruch has an angel hide it in the earth. The Lives of the Prophets repeats the story of Jeremiah, adds that the ark will be raised first at the resurrection, and places it on Sinai. The rabbis offer Josiah, Babylon, or a hiding place under the temple. Chronicles says the ark's poles were there "until today" (2 Chronicles 5:9), and Jeremiah 27:19–22 expects the temple's vessels to go to Babylon and return. Revelation sees "the ark of his covenant" in God's temple in heaven (Revelation 11:19), and promises "the hidden manna" (Revelation 2:17), and many Christian writers have read the next chapter, about the woman clothed with the sun, as its sequel. On Mary as the ark, see the card at 2 Samuel 6.

The letter says Nehemiah "laid the foundation of a library," gathering "the books about the kings and prophets, and David's books, and letters from kings about gifts," and that Judas gathered again what the war had scattered (2:13–14). It is one of the earliest Jewish texts to speak of sacred books in groups, along with the prologue to Sirach (after 132 BC), which speaks of the law, the prophets and the rest that came after them, and Luke 24:44, "the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms."

Roger Beckwith and others read these texts as signs that the Hebrew canon had its shape by the second century BC. Others note that the verse does not mention the law of Moses, that "letters from kings" were not Scripture, and that a collection is not yet a canon. Catholic and Orthodox readers add that Jerusalem's library, which Judas offers to share with Egypt, says nothing about which Greek books the churches later received. Whether 2 Maccabees itself is Scripture is the first card on the book page.

The writer's own preface (2:19–32) follows the habits of Greek historians: a summary of the subject, the name of the source (Jason of Cyrene, in five books), the aim of the work, and a defense of the method. He wants to give "enjoyment," "ease" for those who want to remember, and "benefit" to all (2:25), the two goals Greek and Roman writers set for good writing, pleasure and profit. He returns at the end with the image of wine mixed with water (15:39).

Because he speaks so openly of his labor and his choices, his preface has been at the center of debates about inspiration. Catholic and Orthodox readers answer that God works through human authors' gifts and labor, as Luke also researched (Luke 1:1–4). Many Protestant readers answer that a prophet speaks God's words and does not ask indulgence for his style. The card on the book page sets out the answers.

echoes: Jeremiah 3:16; Jeremiah 10:3–9; Jeremiah 29:1–23; Deuteronomy 34:1–4; Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Kings 8:10–11; Leviticus 9:24; Leviticus 10:16–20; 2 Chronicles 7:1–10; Exodus 19:6; Hebrews 9:3–4; Revelation 11:19; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6; Galatians 1:13–14; Luke 1:1–4; Luke 24:44

settings.to: the people being carried off to Babylon
settings.when: at the exile, 586 BC, as the letter tells it
settings.why: To warn the exiles not to forget the law or be led astray by the gold and silver idols of the nations, and to keep the law in their hearts.
settings.readers: The letter's readers lived among the temples and images of Egypt, as the exiles had lived among those of Babylon. The same warning, in fuller form, is the Letter of Jeremiah, which most scholars date before about 100 BC, since a Greek fragment of it was found at Qumran (7Q2).

settings.what: Jeremiah's words at the hidden cave
settings.to: his companions who tried to mark the way
settings.when: after he hid the tent, the ark and the altar of incense
settings.why: To forbid any search: the place will stay unknown until God gathers his people and shows mercy, and then the glory and the cloud will be seen as in Moses' and Solomon's days.
settings.readers: For Jews of the Diaspora, the words joined the temple's lost vessels to the hope of the gathering that the letter prays for (1:27; 2:18). The story was still told in a later Jewish work, 2 Baruch 6 (about AD 100), which shows how it could be read as a promise about the end.

settings.by: Moses, as the letter quotes him
settings.when: in the wilderness, at the first sacrifices
settings.why: To explain why fire consumed the sin offering: because it had not been eaten, it was burned up.
settings.readers: The saying is not in the law. Readers who knew Leviticus 10:16–20 would hear a version of the story of the burned goat of the sin offering, told to explain the miracle of fire.

settings.by: the epitomist, the unnamed writer who shortened Jason's history
settings.when: probably late in the second century BC, after 161 BC, the last event in the book
settings.why: To introduce the subject, name his source, and explain his method: a short, pleasant summary, leaving exact detail to the historian.
settings.readers: His readers knew Greek and Greek literary habits: the preface uses the language of Hellenistic historians and the Greek ideal of pleasure and profit. Clement of Alexandria, about AD 200, knows the writer as "the composer of the epitome of the Maccabees" (Stromata 5.14.97.7), the oldest notice of the book as an abridgment.

title: Heliodorus and the Temple Treasury
sum: Jerusalem is at peace under the godly high priest Onias, and even the Seleucid king Seleucus IV pays for its sacrifices. Then Simon, the overseer of the temple, quarrels with Onias over the city market and tells the governor Apollonius that the temple treasury holds untold wealth that belongs to the king. Seleucus sends his chief minister Heliodorus to take it. Onias explains that the money belongs to widows and orphans and to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, and that no one may wrong those who trusted the temple.

Heliodorus goes ahead. The priests throw themselves down before the altar, the high priest is pale with grief, women in sackcloth fill the streets, and the whole people pray. At the treasury God makes "a great appearance": a horse with a rider in golden armor charges and kicks Heliodorus, and two splendid young men flog him until he falls. He is carried out helpless. At his friends' request Onias offers a sacrifice for him, and the young men appear again and tell him that he owes his life to the high priest. Heliodorus sacrifices to God, returns to the king, and tells him that if he has an enemy, he should send him to Jerusalem.
readings: Greek temples told stories of gods who defended their treasures against robbers, and this chapter follows the pattern: a royal officer, a threatened treasure, a city at prayer, a sudden appearance, and a confession by the defeated. It shows the reader the rule that governs the book: while the people are faithful, the place is safe.

The golden age does not last. Simon's slander continues (4:1–6), Onias is pushed out by his brother Jason, and in 5:15–21 Antiochus IV robs the temple unharmed. The book explains the difference: "the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (5:19).

views.C: Catholic readers see in the chapter God's care for his house and for the poor whose deposits were kept there. Raphael's fresco The Expulsion of Heliodorus from the Temple (1511–1512), painted in the Vatican for Pope Julius II, made the story an image of God's defense of the Church and its goods against those who would rob it.
views.O: Orthodox readers have taken the horseman and the young men as angels, and the chapter as witness to angels who guard holy places and come to the aid of the faithful. Onias, praying for his enemy, is a model of the priest who intercedes.
views.P: Protestant readers value the chapter's lesson that God hears the prayers of his people and judges the proud, while denying it authority to settle doctrine. On whether a church building is holy, which Calvin denied, see the card below.
views.H: The setting is historical: Seleucus IV, his minister Heliodorus, and a royal drive to control temple funds are confirmed by an inscription of 178 BC. The miracle story itself is legend, and Bickerman argued that two versions of it have been joined. 4 Maccabees 4 tells it of Apollonius, and 3 Maccabees 1–2 tells a similar story of Ptolemy IV.
views.J: The rabbis do not tell the story of Heliodorus, but they remember a priestly family that betrayed the temple in the Greek period: the Mishnah says the division of Bilgah was punished (Mishnah Sukkah 5:8), and the Talmud blames Miriam of the house of Bilgah, who married a Greek soldier (Bavli Sukkah 56b). Some scholars link this with Simon of 3:4, following Latin and Armenian copies that read "Bilgah."

deep.b:
Heliodorus is known outside 2 Maccabees. Inscriptions honor him as the chief minister of Seleucus IV, and in 175 BC, Appian says, he plotted against the king and had him killed (Syrian Wars 45). A stone inscription bought on the antiquities market and published in 2007 by Hannah Cotton and Michael Wörrle preserves a letter of Seleucus IV to Heliodorus, dated 178 BC, appointing a man named Olympiodoros to oversee the temples of "Coele-Syria and Phoenicia." Fragments of the same stone were found in excavations at Maresha in Israel. The letter shows the king tightening control over temple finances in the province, the background against which Simon's report (3:6) would have been welcome.

The king needed money. In the peace of Apamea (188 BC) Rome had forced his father Antiochus III to pay an enormous indemnity in yearly installments, and Antiochus III had died robbing a temple in the east. Daniel 11:20, describing the king who followed Antiochus III, says one "will send a tax-gatherer through the splendor of the kingdom" and soon be broken, "neither in anger nor in battle." Most scholars read this of Seleucus IV and Heliodorus.

Readers have noticed that the miracle seems to happen twice. A horse and rider strike Heliodorus (3:25), and two young men flog him (3:26). He falls, darkness covers him, and he is carried out (3:27–28), yet later the young men appear to him again and speak (3:33–34). Elias Bickerman argued that two versions of the story have been woven together: one in which Heliodorus is trampled and saved only by Onias's sacrifice, and one in which he is flogged by angels and sent away to tell of God's power. Others, including Robert Doran, read the chapter as a single, carefully built account in which each scene has its job.

The story has a long afterlife. 4 Maccabees 4:1–14 retells it with Apollonius as the officer, and 3 Maccabees tells a similar story of Ptolemy IV at the temple. Raphael painted it in the Vatican (1511–1512), and Eugène Delacroix in the church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris (1856–1861).

Onias III, son of the high priest Simon II whom Sirach praises (Sirach 50:1–21), is the book's model of a godly high priest. In this chapter he defends the deposits of widows and orphans and then prays for the man who came to rob them. In chapter 4 his brother Jason buys the office from Antiochus IV (4:7–10), and about 170 BC Onias is murdered near Antioch at the order of Menelaus (4:33–35). In Judas's dream before his last battle, Onias is seen praying for the whole people (15:12–14).

Josephus says that a son of Onias fled to Egypt and, with the leave of Ptolemy VI, built a temple at Leontopolis, appealing to Isaiah's prophecy that the LORD would have "an altar in the heart of the land of Egypt" (Isaiah 19:19; Antiquities 13.62–73). It stood until the Romans closed it in AD 73 (Jewish War 7.420–436). Many scholars think the book's praise of Onias and its letters about Jerusalem's feast speak to Jews in Egypt who knew that temple. On the family, see the topic page.

settings.by: Simon, the overseer of the temple
settings.to: Apollonius, governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia
settings.why: To get the better of Onias by telling the king's governor that the treasury held vast funds that had nothing to do with the sacrifices and could pass to the king.
settings.readers: The book's readers would know where such a report led: Simon's brother Menelaus later bought the high priesthood and robbed the temple (4:23–32). An inscription of 178 BC shows that the king was in fact appointing officials over the temples of the province, so the report fell on willing ears.

settings.why: To show that the money was not the king's: it was held in trust for widows and orphans and for Hyrcanus son of Tobias, and to wrong those who trusted a temple honored all over the world would be impossible.
settings.readers: The answer argues both from the law of Moses (the widow and orphan) and from Greek law (the temple's right of sanctuary), as the book's readers in the Greek world would expect. Josephus confirms that Hyrcanus the Tobiad was a powerful figure east of the Jordan until 175 BC (Antiquities 12.228–236).

settings.by: the priests in their robes, the high priest, and the whole people
settings.to: God, "the one who gave the law about money left in trust"
settings.when: on the day Heliodorus entered the treasury
settings.why: To ask God to keep the deposits safe for their owners and to protect the place from contempt.
settings.readers: The scene of a city in sackcloth, with even the secluded young women in the streets, became a model: 3 Maccabees 1:16–2:20 describes the same kind of scene when Ptolemy IV tries to enter the holy of holies, which shows that Jewish readers in Egypt knew and reused the pattern.

settings.what: The young men's message to Heliodorus
settings.by: the two young men, now seen to be heavenly
settings.when: while Onias was offering the sacrifice for him
settings.why: To tell him that he owes his life to Onias and must tell everyone how great God's power is.
settings.readers: The book makes the message an argument to its readers: the high priest's prayer saved even the temple's enemy, and near its end the book shows Onias, now dead, praying for the whole people in Judas's dream (15:12–14).

settings.why: To warn the king that God guards the temple: anyone sent there to harm it will come back flogged, if he comes back at all.
settings.readers: Readers who knew that Heliodorus later plotted against Seleucus, as Appian reports (Syrian Wars 45), could hear irony in his advice to send the king's enemies to Jerusalem. The chapters that follow test his claim when Antiochus IV robs the temple and is not struck down at once (5:15–21).

traditions.q: Heliodorus says that the God who lives in heaven watches over the temple in Jerusalem and strikes those who come to harm it (3:38–39). Are some places on earth holy now, such as consecrated churches, altars and shrines, so that God is present or hears prayer there in a special way? Jesus said that the hour was coming when the Father would be worshiped neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem (John 4:21–23). (Whether the saints in heaven pray for us is asked at Revelation 5.)
views: Yes, in a real but subordinate sense. The Catechism teaches that Christ is the true temple and that God's worship is not tied to one place, yet church buildings are holy places: they are images of the heavenly Jerusalem and houses of prayer, where the Eucharist is celebrated, and Christ is present in the tabernacle (Catechism 1179, 1183, 1197–1199). Canon law defines sacred places as those set apart for worship or burial by dedication or blessing (canon 1205), and the Church encourages pilgrimage to shrines.

Yes. God's grace works through matter and through the places where he acted. John of Damascus wrote that he would never cease to honor the matter through which his salvation came, naming Calvary, the life-giving tomb and the wood of the cross (On the Divine Images 1.16). Consecrated churches and holy places are honored for that reason, not as gods but as filled with God's grace.

A church is set apart by its use, not by a holiness of its own. Dedicating the castle church at Torgau in 1544, Luther said that nothing should happen there except that the Lord speaks to his people through his holy word and they answer him in prayer and praise. The building is not holier than any other place where the word is preached.

No place is holier than another under the gospel. The Westminster Confession says that prayer and worship are not now tied to any place or made more acceptable by it, and that God is to be worshiped everywhere in spirit and truth (21.6). Calvin warned against thinking churches "the proper dwellings of God," with "some kind of secret sanctity": "we are the true temples of God" (Institutes 3.20.30).
